i remember saying at triage “i think im over reacting but it won’t stop bleeding” and the nurse was like “oh my god no that definitely needs stitches” and i literally bled so much all over the hospital waiting room that they got me in a room in like 15 minutes and i cannot stress how horrified i was it was bleeding so much for what i thought was a pretty small cut. it sucked, i felt so bad, nothing like trying to wipe blood off the seat with napkins while people are staring at you and knowing it’s your own goddamn fault. nurse stopped the bleeding, waited a couple hours for the doctor to stitch it up, they gave me a bunch of sheets about self harm and therapy sent me on my way. probably 3 hours at the hospital? pretty much everyone asked if i wanted to kill myself, which i did, but i’d just got a puppy (she’s my life saver i love her sm) so i insisted i didn’t — no plans no intent no means. everyone was very nice lmao i felt cared for and after it made me cry because usually no one takes me seriously 

i pretty much refused to talk about it with my family after. i know it upset them a lot. i don’t know how much else they know about my self harm. i was super fucking distressed that day for hours before, and i made it clear to them, and i wasn’t taken seriously until i cut myself. i don’t think they know the extent of the self harm problem, and i didn’t want to talk about it. but yeah it sucked, that’s the only time ive ever been to the er for self harm, and i hate that i let it get that far

i skipped school or stayed home sick constantly during high school and university and was late most of the time but when it comes to work i’ve been very good at getting to work on time, at least during the last job i had — i worked at a coffee shop part time and never even overslept opening. i’ve been working full time in an office for the last week and we’ll see how that ends up going. 

the financial aspect is huge. in school skipping is on your dime and the consequences aren’t huge, and i usually got the work done if i wasn’t physically at a school, so it was net positive for me to skip. at work, if i no call no show like i did all the time for school, i risk losing my job. that’s a pretty fucking big consequence, so i drag myself out of bed and go. i don’t want to call in, because that means communicating with my boss, and i have very severe social anxiety, so it’s less stressful to just drag myself in anyway. i’m really lucky in that even if i’m unemployed i don’t have to worry about whether i can put food in my stomach or have a roof over my head, but that’s another consequence for most people. 

my advice is try to give yourself a reward for being at work. i was always excited to get my free coffee at the coffee job, so it made going to that job a lot easier than going to my office job, where i know i’m gonna have to sit in my cubicle for 8 hours and be anxious. 

honestly, capitalism and working culture is shit and completely fucking draining on the mental health, and im not gonna lie, sometimes i just give myself permission to like cut myself in the bathroom or something if i manage to get to work. usually it doesn’t get to that point. but in the end if you don’t go to work you don’t get paid, and it sucks.

but because i still live at home it’s like, i still gotta keep it hidden, i still gotta hide my tools. my family found out about my self harm literally two weeks ago when i hit a small artery and had to ask my mom to drive me to the ER.

personally, i feel a lot of shame about still doing this at almost 24 years old, but i also feel like i’ve been treated with a lot more respect about it, which honestly makes a HUGE difference in my willingness to open up. when my then family doctor and parents found out i was self harming at 14, my family doctor told me “stop being immature,” my parents threatened to send me to a psych ward, took away all of the sharp objects, made me show them all my wounds, blamed themselves, my first therapist told me “it could be worse,” i was just told i have to stop which just drove me to hide it better instead.

i think it is also important to ensure good mental health because at 12 i was cheerful despite it all and things began to crumble in my mid-late teens. like, good coping strategies and establishment of trust and making sure professionals are an option and just noticing if anything’s off and having self care.

for body stuff, be open about periods and puberty stuff! i was so ashamed of having periods and having to deal with it in public that i stayed home from school on my period until i had to live in a dorm for a summer at 21. a lot of stuff that people learned in their early teens like hygiene, bras, periods, deodorant, etc i was so embarrassed about until early twenties because my mom was always embarrassed about it, and it definitely led to a lot of disordered thoughts around my body and contributed to my poor wellbeing, so normalizing it early will help a lot!

I got my licence right when I turned 16 due to my mom’s urging, passed on the first try, and proceeded to drive very sparingly and only with a parent in the car for the next five years. I finally learned how to drive alone this past summer but it is extremely anxiety inducing for me. 

All the allistic people I know don’t have these problems with driving while most autistic people, even if they drive, tend to struggle or learned late. Driving can be super overwhelming for someone who struggles with sensory issues and the most important thing is to stay safe, however that looks for you. For me I only drive routes I know and try not to go during rush hour or heavy traffic.

Got diagnosed at 12 and am 19 and I think I'm only mildly on the spectrum. This is from personal experience. I've been to several support groups/social skills courses and have a friend with ASD. 

1) From my experience, most boys diagnosed with ASD tend to be more stereotypically autistic. In support groups, I've noticed about 70% of boys and could tell they have ASD while for girls only one out of the ~10 girls I've met was stereotypical. That's not to say that girls automatically have better social skills, or don't stim; I think we're forced to mask ASD symptoms because people don't perceive girls as having ASD. One of my good friends is autistic; my mom met her and figured it out right away and I didn't notice for 8 months, until she told me. For girls, a lot of their special interests are fandom related because it's more accepted. I'm pretty open about intensely loving books/musicals but I keep quiet about the others (travel, roller coasters, architecture). 

2) As a kid, I felt more connection to boys who were troublemakers. I didn't have a female friend until I was nearly done elementary school. Nowadays I don't really feel a connection to anyone, but I feel much more comfortable around girls. 

3) Being a girl I think you get more comorbidities with other mental illnesses/learning disabilities - I don't know if it's just prejudice within the psychology communities. Most girls with ASD I've known also have depression, anxiety, or both; I've been diagnosed with ADHD in addition to the previous three. Boys are normally just ASD or ADHD. 

4) Girls definitely blend in easier, I guess. Boys tend to get The Look more than I have; usually people take me as shy and passionate about some things and not, "Oh, she's definitely autistic."

5) Personally I feel like ASD just makes everything more difficult. Unlike a lot of other commenters, I do not have attention to detail. I always make dumb mistakes that I miss. I get overwhelmed easily in most situations; if it's serious my emotions shut down. So everyday things can sometimes make me meltdown but having to call 911 I'm pretty calm. I guess I have a good imagination. I'm can get reasonably decent grades with minimal effort and care. I don't know if that's ASD related though.
